notes.meaning: Sarah lived to the age of 127. She is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded, showing the high honor God gave to the mother of His chosen people. Her long life had seen God faithfully fulfill His promise of a son.

Sarah died at Hebron, then called Kiriath-arba, in the land of Canaan. Abraham wept aloud and observed the customary time of mourning for his wife. His grief was sincere and deep, yet he mourned with quiet trust in God's promises.

After sitting in grief beside his wife's body, Abraham rose to make arrangements for her burial. He went to the local Hittite leaders who owned and governed the area. Caring for practical duties was his next act of love and respect for Sarah.

Abraham explained to the Hittites that he was a foreigner living among them with no land of his own. He asked them for the right to buy a burial plot so he could lay his wife to rest. Although God had promised the entire land to his future family, Abraham still lived as a pilgrim on earth.

The Hittites answered Abraham with great respect, calling him a prince of God or an honored leader among them. They offered him the free choice of their finest tombs to bury his dead. They were eager to show him kindness, though they offered only the use of an existing grave rather than selling him permanent land.

Abraham stood up and bowed low before the people of the land to thank them for their generous offer. He followed the proper local customs of courtesy and showed deep honor to his neighbors. True faith teaches good manners, gratitude, and respect toward others.

Abraham asked the city leaders to speak with a man named Ephron about purchasing the cave of Machpelah. He did not want to borrow a grave, but insisted on paying the full price so his family would own a permanent burial site. Machpelah lay at the edge of Ephron's field and would provide a lasting resting place.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition, following the Latin Vulgate, translates Machpelah as the 'double cave,' seeing it as a cavern divided into two chambers.

notes.meaning: Ephron was sitting among the Hittite leaders at the city gate, which was the public center for legal rulings and business trade. Hearing Abraham's request, Ephron spoke up directly so that everyone present could hear the terms.

Ephron offered to give Abraham both the cave and the field around it as an outright gift before all his people. In ancient Eastern business, offering land as a gift was polite speech that opened the door to a transaction. It also shifted the discussion from just the cave to the entire field.

Abraham bowed once again before the assembled townspeople. This courteous bow showed his appreciation for Ephron's words while signaling that he still had more to say. He conducted the entire negotiation with calm dignity and humility.

Abraham spoke directly to Ephron and firmly insisted on paying the full purchase price for the field. He did not want to take advantage of his neighbor's polite offer or leave his family indebted to others. Wisdom and honesty led Abraham to make a clear, clean purchase.

Ephron named the price of four hundred shekels of silver, while casually adding that such a sum was nothing between two friends. Four hundred shekels was a very high price for land at that time. Even so, naming the figure allowed the legal deal to move forward without further delay.

Abraham accepted the price immediately and weighed out the silver in front of all the witnesses. Since stamped coins did not yet exist, the silver had to be weighed according to the standard used by local merchants. Abraham paid the full amount openly and without trying to haggle.

The field at Machpelah, the cave inside it, and all the trees within its boundaries were legally deeded to Abraham. The transaction took place publicly at the city gate before all the citizens who had gathered. This public agreement ensured that no one could later challenge Abraham's legal ownership.

After the land was legally secured, Abraham laid Sarah to rest in the cave of Machpelah near Mamre in Hebron. This site became the sacred resting place of the patriarchs. Years later, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were all buried in this same cave.

The field and its cave were fully established as Abraham's permanent property for a burial site. This small plot was the only piece of the promised land Abraham ever owned in his lifetime. Buying it demonstrated his deep faith that God would one day give the whole country to his descendants.
